summary: Port Greville's 1907 wooden range tower was lit in 1908, dismantled and moved to Sydney in 1981, and returned to the Age of Sail Heritage Centre in 1998.

structures.type: A-shaped square wood tower with balcony and square lantern
structures.note: Register and the 1908 Chief Engineer report give 8.3 m (27 ft). Lighthouse Friends and Rowlett give 25 ft (7.5 m) to the lantern ventilator.

structures.type: pole light with shed at the outer end of the breakwater
structures.note: Set up in 1917; breakwater rebuilt and a pole light placed at its outer end in 1926; front light destroyed in 1940 (Lighthouse Friends).

access.note: On the grounds of the Age of Sail Heritage Centre beside Route 209. Grounds open; tower open in season (Lighthouse Friends; Rowlett).

events.note: Round timber cribwork about 671 m (2,200 ft) long built along the gravel bar to protect the harbour
Built by contract, John D. Reid of Wallace Bay, $790
Lit in 1908 (kerosene), with a front light and a back light in range
Ernest A. Hatfield appointed first keeper of the range lights, 29 June 1908 (checked in the 1909, 1910, 1911 and 1916 statements)

Pole front light with shed placed near the breakwater's outer end; the enclosed tower became the rear light and changed from red to white (Lighthouse Friends). Rowlett dates the rear change to the 1920s.
Freshet undermined the breakwater at Port Greville; a wire dispatch says the lighthouse slid into the channel while unoccupied. Which light is not stated; Lighthouse Friends does not mention it.
Breakwater rebuilt; pole light placed at its outer end as the new front range light
Front light destroyed; the cause is not given
Groundhog Day gale, 2 February 1976, swept into Port Greville and destroyed the Wagstaff & Hatfield shipyard
Inactive since 1976 (Rowlett). The register dates the decommissioning to 1980.
Tower sawn in half and trucked to the Canadian Coast Guard College, Sydney, Cape Breton; the register dates the move to 1980
Returned to Port Greville, reassembled, open on the Age of Sail Heritage Centre grounds in August 1998
Re-clad in clapboard over the existing shingles; new railing around the lantern the following spring

corrections.why: The tower was built by contract in 1907 (Lighthouse Friends; the 1908 Chief Engineer report; the register gives built 1907). The 1908 date is the year the light was first shown (register, Lighthouse Friends, Rowlett, NSLPS).
The register and the 1908 report give 8.3 m (27 ft). Lighthouse Friends and Rowlett give 7.5 m (25 ft); both figures are recorded in the note.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The register, Lighthouse Friends and the 1908 Chief Engineer's report put the work in 1907 (contract by John D. Reid), and the light was first shown in 1908 (register, Lighthouse Friends, NSLPS). Rowlett gives 1908 as the single year in its entry. Both years belong to the story: built 1907, first lit 1908.

notes_for_editor: (1) Tower height disagrees: 27 ft (8.3 m) in the 1908 Chief Engineer report (checked on the page image, printed p. 64) and the register; 25 ft (7.5 m) in Lighthouse Friends and Rowlett. The story gives both. The structure record keeps 8.3 m because it rests on the primary report. (2) Deactivation and move disagree: Rowlett says inactive since 1976; the register says decommissioned, cut in two and moved in 1980; Lighthouse Friends, NSLPS and Rowlett give the move as 1981. The record's 1976 deactivated stays unless a human picks 1980. (3) Apparatus: Lighthouse Friends gives the front (enclosed tower) a sixth-order dioptric apparatus and the back an anchor lens lantern on two 15 ft poles. The official list of new lights for 1907-08 (checked on the page image, printed p. 87) gives the front light an anchor lantern and the back a fifth-order French lens. The story reports both; it does not call them reversed. (4) Rear change: Lighthouse Friends says 1917 (with the colour change to white); Rowlett says the 1920s after a channel shift. (5) Keeper appointment: Lighthouse Friends and the 1909, 1910, 1911 and 1916 statements give 29 June 1908. All four statement rows were checked on the page images; the 1911 OCR prints 'June 20' and the image reads 'June 29'. Station-to-name matching in the four statements is by OCR column position and was confirmed on the images. (6) Shared surname: keeper Ernest A. Hatfield and shipbuilder Otto Hatfield (Wagstaff & Hatfield) share a surname. No source links them. Do not join them. (7) Shipyard dates: Age of Sail Heritage Centre pages and Shipbuilding History say Otto Hatfield joined George Wagstaff in 1933; Lighthouse Friends says the firm was formed in 1933. The Department's 1917 monthly list (checked on the page image, printed p. 13) and the fiscal 1917-18 wooden shipbuilding plant list (checked, printed p. 22) already name 'Wagstaff & Hatfield, Port Greville'. The Centre says George Wagstaff moved to Port Greville around 1916. The story reports both and does not settle it. (8) Ownership: Lighthouse Friends says the village owns it and the museum manages it; NSLPS says the community museum owns it. (9) Visibility distances (6 miles, 9 miles elsewhere) are not stated as nautical. (10) Opening times are from Rowlett and Lighthouse Friends and may be out of date; check the museum. (11) The register's '2001 municipal' and 'Current function Museum' come from the Heritage Guide copy of entry 11321; the register page itself gave the register text only. Lighthouse Friends says it was placed on the Canadian Register in 2009; not checked here. (12) DeWolfe is named only as Lighthouse Friends gives him (1950s to 1960s); no further detail. (13) OCR: the 1908 official list reads 'Frencli' and 'Bach Light' in the corpus text; the page image reads 'French lens' and 'Back Light'. Quotes keep the OCR text. (14) Newspapers: Chronicling America returned 163 pages for 'Port Greville' (1880-1930). Only one was read and used: the St. Croix Avis wire item of 4 May 1923 (note 15). (15) The 1923 breakwater and lighthouse event rests on one wire dispatch printed in the St. Croix Avis of Christiansted (4 May 1923, p. 3, read through newspapers.py). The OCR reads 'by the freshest caused by the melting snow and heavy rains of yesterday'; 'freshet' in the story is the editor's reading of that OCR word and is not confirmed on the page image. No Canadian annual report or other source in this research mentions the event, and Lighthouse Friends does not. The dispatch does not say which light slid into the channel; the story says so. (16) Fiscal years: the 1909 volume's annual report covers fiscal 1907-08, which the volume says was the fiscal year ending March 31 (the earlier label 'ended 30 June 1908' was wrong). The 1919 volume is the fiscal year 1917-18 (earlier label 'ended 30 June 1918' was wrong). The 1911 volume's statement is printed p. 257 (scan p. 259). (17) Verification pass 2026-10-27: the 'Other sources call the river the Greville River' sentence now names the Heritage Guide and NSLPS as the sources for the Greville River name, and records that Lighthouse Friends says Ratchford; the 1923 freshet sentence now carries its footnote; the Lighthouse Friends 'does not mention' claim is footnoted; the keeper plea is not attributed to Hatfield (the sources do not name the keeper); the Chief Engineer's report period, the 1909 list label, and the 1919 fiscal year are corrected; the register's 1980 and Lighthouse Friends' 1981 are stated as a disagreement; Wikidata is removed from resolved_conflicts because it is not a cited source.
